es.summary: Los AINEs inhiben las enzimas COX‑1 y COX‑2, reduciendo la síntesis de prostaglandinas y, por ende, la inflamación, el dolor y la fiebre.
key_points: Efectos adversos principales: gastritis/úlcera, hemorragia y nefrotoxicidad.
No deben usarse en pacientes con insuficiencia renal aguda o úlcera péptica activa.
Pueden interferir con anticoagulantes y antihipertensivos.
Monitorear signos de sangrado y función renal durante el tratamiento.

mechanism: Bloquean la enzima ciclooxigenasa (COX‑1 y/o COX‑2).
Disminuyen la producción de prostaglandinas proinflamatorias.
Reducen la sensibilización de los nociceptores al dolor.
contraindications: Úlcera péptica activa o historial de sangrado gastrointestinal.
adverse_effects: Edema y aumento de presión arterial (común).
Reacciones cutáneas graves como síndrome de Stevens‑Johnson (serio).
interactions: Aumenta el riesgo de sangrado con anticoagulantes (warfarina, heparina).
Potencia la nefrotoxicidad con inhibidores de la ECA y diuréticos.
Reduce la eficacia de antihipertensivos (IECA, betabloqueadores).
Puede aumentar niveles de litio y metotrexato.
nursing_care: Evaluar historial de úlcera, función renal (creatinina, BUN) y presión arterial antes de iniciar.
Monitorear signos de sangrado: hematoquecia, melena, hematuria.
Controlar creatinina y electrolitos cada 48‑72 h en pacientes de riesgo.
Retener la dosis si la presión arterial supera 140/90 mmHg sin control.
Notificar al médico si aparecen dolor abdominal intenso o sangrado visible.
patient_teaching: Tomar el medicamento con alimentos o antiácidos para proteger el estómago.
Evitar alcohol y tabaco mientras se usa el AINE.
Reportar cualquier sangrado inusual, dolor abdominal o disminución de la micción.
Informar al profesional de salud sobre otros fármacos que esté tomando.

outcomes: Sin evidencia de hemorragia gastrointestinal en 48 h
Hemoglobina estable (variación < 1 g/dL) durante la hospitalización

interventions.action: Evaluar signos de sangrado (hematoquecia, melena, hematomas) al ingreso y cada 4 h.
Obtener hemograma completo y niveles de hemoglobina cada 24 h.
Administrar protector gástrico (p. ej., omeprazol 20 mg VO cada 24 h) según indicación médica.
interventions.rationale: Reduce riesgo de ulceración y sangrado.

interventions.action: Retener AINE si el paciente presenta presión arterial > 150/100 mmHg o signos de sangrado.
Educar al paciente sobre la importancia de reportar cualquier cambio en el color de las heces o vómitos.
interventions.rationale: Facilita la detección precoz de hemorragia.

en.summary: NSAIDs inhibit COX‑1 and COX‑2 enzymes, reducing prostaglandin synthesis and thereby inflammation, pain, and fever.
key_points: Main adverse effects: gastritis/ulcer, bleeding, nephrotoxicity.
Should not be used in patients with acute renal failure or active peptic ulcer.
Can interfere with anticoagulants and antihypertensives.
Monitor for bleeding signs and renal function during treatment.

mechanism: Block the cyclooxygenase enzyme (COX‑1 and/or COX‑2).
contraindications: Active peptic ulcer or history of gastrointestinal bleeding.
adverse_effects: Severe skin reactions such as Stevens‑Johnson syndrome (serious).
interactions: Increases bleeding risk with anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin).
Potentiates nephrotoxicity with ACE inhibitors and diuretics.
Reduces efficacy of antihypertensives (ACE inhibitors, beta‑blockers).
May increase levels of lithium and methotrexate.
nursing_care: Assess ulcer history, renal function (creatinine, BUN), and blood pressure before starting.
Monitor for bleeding signs: hematochezia, melena, hematuria.
Check creatinine and electrolytes every 48‑72 h in at‑risk patients.
Hold dose if blood pressure exceeds 140/90 mmHg without control.
Notify the physician if severe abdominal pain or visible bleeding occurs.
patient_teaching: Take the medication with food or antacids to protect the stomach.
Avoid alcohol and tobacco while using NSAIDs.
Report any unusual bleeding, abdominal pain, or decreased urine output.
Do not combine multiple NSAIDs simultaneously.
Inform the healthcare professional of all other medications you are taking.

outcomes: No evidence of gastrointestinal bleeding within 48 h

interventions.action: Assess bleeding signs (hematochezia, melena, bruising) upon admission and every 4 h.
Obtain complete blood count and hemoglobin levels every 24 h.
Administer gastric protector (e.g., omeprazole 20 mg PO daily) as ordered.
Hold NSAID if patient has blood pressure > 150/100 mmHg or signs of bleeding.
Educate patient on importance of reporting any changes in stool color or vomiting.

sources.name: Pharmacology for Nurses: Introduction to the Inflammatory Response and Anti-inflammatory Drugs

summary.0.quote: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs ( NSAIDs ) inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes.

sections.mechanism.0.quote: Cyclooxygenase has two major isoforms: COX-1 and COX-2.

sections.mechanism.1.quote: COX causes this increase in inflammation and pain by increasing the production of cytokines such as prostaglandins, prostacyclin, and thromboxane.

sections.mechanism.2.quote: These agents generally work by inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX), a major pro-inflammatory enzyme that causes many signs and symptoms of inflammation, including redness, swelling, and sensitization of nociceptors, thereby increasing the transmission of painful signals to the brain.

sections.indications.0.quote: It is one of the most popular analgesics due to its low cost, efficacy in treating mild to moderate pain, and excellent safety profile when used within the recommended dosages.

sections.contraindications.0.quote: Older adults and individuals with a prior history of peptic ulcer disease or gastrointestinal bleeding are at greater risk for serious gastrointestinal events.

sections.contraindications.2.quote: Contraindications include hypersensitivity to the drug or any of its components; having a history of allergies, asthma, or urticaria (hives) after taking aspirin or other NSAIDs; coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery; and with celecoxib sulfonamide allergy.

sections.adverse_effects.0.quote: Adverse Effects Abdominal pain Dyspepsia Peripheral edema Dizziness Rash Hepatotoxicity Renal toxicity GI bleeding Thrombocythemia Bronchospasm Photosensitivity Contraindications Hypersensitivity History

sections.adverse_effects.1.quote: NSAIDs also increased the risk of serious gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events including bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal.

sections.adverse_effects.2.quote: Common adverse effects of NSAIDs include gastrointestinal issues (stomach pain, heartburn, indigestion, nausea, GI bleeding), headache, dizziness, fluid retention, high blood pressure, renal and liver impairment, and an increased risk of cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke.

sections.interactions.0.quote: Nurses should instruct clients taking blood thinners (e.g., warfarin, apixaban) to be cautious about using aspirin to treat pain because of increased risk for bleeding and bruising.

sections.nursing_care.4.quote: Clients reporting severe abdominal pain, dark tarry stools, or vomiting or coughing up of blood should stop using any NSAIDs immediately and be assessed by a health care provider for possible stomach ulcers.

sections.patient_teaching.2.quote: Clients reporting severe abdominal pain, dark tarry stools, or vomiting or coughing up of blood should stop using any NSAIDs immediately and be assessed by a health care provider for possible stomach ulcers.

sections.patient_teaching.4.quote: nurses must be alert for all sources of acetaminophen that clients may be taking.
